extracted.intended_audience: microbiologists, microbial taxonomists, and authors proposing or describing prokaryote names
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and recommendations for forming and publishing names of prokaryotes (generic names, specific epithets, names from geography/people/chemicals/arbitrary sources), plus conventions for infrasubspecific designations and the provisional status Candidatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinization of personal names ending in -us
rubrics_metrics.description: Some personal names in Europe were already Latinized before 1800 and kept since. If they end in -us, replace the ending by -a or -ella (diminutive) respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the name Bucerius would result in ‘Buceria’ or ‘Buceriella’. Beware, however, of Lithuanian names like Didlaukus, Zeikus, etc. These are not Latinized but genuine forms and would receive the ending -ia according to Table 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-person limitation for honourific names
rubrics_metrics.description: Not more than one person can be honoured in one generic name or epithet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal names must appear fully (no shortening); omit titles
rubrics_metrics.description: If an organism is named after a person, the name cannot be shortened but must appear fully. Personal titles (Sir, Lord, Duke, Baron, Graf, Conte, etc.) are not included in prokaryote names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘Wigglesia’ after Wigglesworth, ‘Stackia’ after Stackebrandt, ‘Goodfellia’ after Goodfellow. Prefixes and particles treated as described (see separate prefixes rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Scottish patronymic prefixes (Mac, Mc, M)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scottish patronymic prefixes ‘Mac’, ‘Mc’ and ‘M’, meaning ‘son of’, should be written ‘mac’ and be united with the rest of the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘Macdonellia’ or ‘macdonellii’ after MacDonell; Macginleya or macginleyi after McGinley.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Irish patronymic prefix O'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Irish patronymic prefix ‘O’ should be united with the rest of the name or omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘Oconnoria’ or ‘Connoria’ or ‘oconnorii’ or ‘connorii’ after O’Connor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of prefixes that are articles (de, da, le, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prefix consisting of an article or containing an article may be omitted or united to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rochalimaea after da Rocha-Lima; Leclercia or ‘leclercii’ after Le Clerc; Leminorella or leminorii after Le Minor; Deleya or deleyi after de Ley; Devosia or ‘devosii’ after De Vos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Dutch/German prefixes (van, von, van der, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dutch prefix ‘van’ and the German prefix ‘von’ may be omitted or united to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Escherichia after von Escherich; Leeuwenhoekia after van Leeuwenhoek; itersonii after van Iterson; prowazekii after von Prowazek; ‘Vannielia’ or vannielii after van Niel; ‘Vandertoornia’ or ‘vandertoornii’ or ‘Toornia’ or ‘toornii’ after van der Toorn; ‘Vandammella’ or ‘vandammei’ after Vandamme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of 'Saint' (San, Sankt, Santo, etc.) in family names
rubrics_metrics.description: The adjective Saint as part of some family names may be omitted or united to the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘Exuperya’ or ‘exuperyi’ after Saint-Exupéry, ‘Sanmartinia’ or ‘sanmartinii’ after San Martin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of generic names from forenames
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely, generic names or specific epithets have been formed from forenames (first names, given names). First names may be chosen to avoid rather long family names or unusually long (hyphenated) double names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Erwinia named after Erwin F. Smith; Staphylococcus arlettae from Arlette van de Kerckhove.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraction for very frequent family names
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of very frequent family names where the honoured person is not easily identifiable, first and family name may be contracted without connecting vowel or hyphenation, but otherwise treated like a single family name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Owenweeksia, Elizabethkingia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to form generic names from personal names (Table-based endings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide appropriate Latinized endings or diminutives when forming generic names from personal names (examples and endings listed in Table 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 lists direct formation and diminutive formation with various added endings (e.g., add -ea, -a, -ia, add -ella, -lla, -iella, etc.) with many examples such as Beneckea, Burkella, Wangia, Salmonella, Escherichia, Zeikusia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal possibilities for specific epithets from personal names
rubrics_metrics.description: To form specific epithets from personal names there are principally two possibilities: the adjective form and the genitive noun form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The adjective form has no means to recognize the sex of the honoured person. The personal names receive appropriate endings according to the gender of the generic name as indicated in Table 3. When the genitive of a Latinized personal name is formed, the sex of the person may be taken into consideration as indicated in Table 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of specific epithets in adjective form (endings by gender)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjective-form specific epithets add gendered endings to the stem of the personal name as indicated in Table 3 (masculine -ianus/-nus/-anus, feminine -iana/-na/-ana, neuter -ianum/-num/-anum, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kondratieva -> Kondratievianus/anum etc.; Lee -> Leeanus/leeana etc.; Bianchi -> Bianchianus/Bianchiana etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of specific epithets as genitive nouns (endings depend on name ending and sex)
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming genitive nouns for specific epithets, choose appropriate genitive endings based on classical/medieval/Neo-Latin usage and the ending of the original name; different forms may be chosen and present problems for names ending in -a and -o.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 4 gives mappings such as: -a → female -ae, male -ae or -i (varies); -i → -ii; -o → -onis etc. Examples: Suzuki -> suzukii; Otto -> ottonis; Zeikus -> zeikusii; Kondratieva examples shown in table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply genus-name recommendations/rules to specific epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: The recommendations and rules for genus names are also applicable for specific epithets (see D (3), (c)–(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate examples are given in the genus-name section; e.g., prefix handling and Latinization conventions apply equally to epithets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical names: no geopolitical meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The formation of prokaryote names from geographical names has no geopolitical meaning; such names cannot be used to express geopolitical claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical epithets must be adjectives (not genitives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epithets on the basis of geographical names cannot be formed as substantives in the genitive case. They must be adjectives, usually constructed by adding -ensis (masculine/feminine) or -ense (neuter) to the geographical name in agreement with gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If locality ends in -a, -e or -en, drop those letters before adding -ensis/-ense (e.g., jenensis from Jena, californiensis from California). If locality ends in -o, ending becomes -nensis/-nense (e.g., sapporonensis from Sapporo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing classical/Neo-Latin adjectives for places when available
rubrics_metrics.description: Where classical Greek, Latin or medieval Latin adjectives for localities exist they may be used as specific epithets to indicate geographical origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aegyptius (Egypt), africanus (Africa), americanus (America), japonicus (Japan), etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate use of classical or Neo-Latin adjectives for historic place names
rubrics_metrics.description: European and Mediterranean cities and places of classical times may have older Latin names and adjectives; either the classical adjective or the Neo-Latin adjective of the modern name may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lucentum (Alicante) -> lucentensis or alicantensis; Lutetia (Paris) -> lutetiensis or parisensis; Londinium (London) -> londiniensis or londonensis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming epithets from multi-word localities
rubrics_metrics.description: Localities composed of two words (adjective + substantive or two substantives) may form awkward adjectival epithets; options include translating to Latin and forming genitive substantives concatenated, or concatenating the components without hyphenation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lac usprofundi (of Deep Lake), marisnigri (of the Black Sea), vallismortis (of Death Valley). Note: in Latin the basic noun comes first, the determining word second.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inclusion of articles in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclusion of articles (the, el, o, il, le, la, de, der, die, das, den, het, los, las, etc.) as used in some languages should be avoided when forming names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles would unnecessarily elongate names without adding information. Examples: La Paz, El Ferrol, Le Havre, The Netherlands, Den Haag, Los Angeles should avoid carrying the article into the epithet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names for organisms living in association: use genitive of associated organism
rubrics_metrics.description: For names of prokaryotes that live in association or symbiosis with other biota, the easiest way is to use the genitive case of the generic name of the associated organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: suis, equi, bovis, muscae, muris, aquilae, falconis, gypis, elephantis; or fagi, quercus, castaneae, aesculi, ros ae, liliae. Use plural genitive when several host species may house the prokaryote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to use plural genitive for host-associated names when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatively the genitive of the plural is recommendable, especially if several species of the associated (usually) eukaryotic genus house the prokaryote species in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To form the plural genitive one needs to know the stem and declension of the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Latin/Neo-Latin stems for names from other languages; transform Greek endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Names originating from languages other than Latin or Greek should not be taken unless they may be constructed from Latin or Greek word stems. Only Latin gender endings are permitted; Greek endings must be transformed into Latin endings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Swahili simba could have been Latinized as leonis (of the lion) rather than simbae. When unavoidable, the word stem must be identified before Latinization (e.g., Arabic al-qaliy -> kalium origin explanation). Do not carry over typical usages of other languages into Latin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declension guidance for genitives of non-Latin words
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide declension endings of Latin genitives for common declensions to assist forming genitives from foreign stems (1st: -arum; 2nd: -orum; 3rd consonant stems: -um; 3rd vocal/mixed: -ium; 4th: -um; 5th: -rum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note irregular forms and use dictionaries. Examples and notes on irregulars like bos -> bovis, canis -> canis given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Englishified suffixes; use classical Neo-Latin endings (e.g., -philus not -philicus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The English suffix -philic should not be carried into Neo-Latin; use -philus/-a/-um rather than -philicus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hydrophilic (English) corresponds to hydrophilus in Neo-Latin; therefore ending -philicus must be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinize national food or fermentation product names as neuter nouns with -um
rubrics_metrics.description: National foods or fermentation products often lacking Latin equivalents should be Latinized by forming a neuter substantive by adding -um and the genitive of that (ending -i) used in the specific epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sake -> sakeum -> epithet sakei; tofu -> tofuum -> tofui; kefir -> kefirum -> kefiri; pombe -> pombeum -> pombei.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latinization rules for names of elements and chemical compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Most names of chemicals are Latinized as neuter nouns of the 2nd declension ending -um with genitives in -i. Different chemical name endings are grouped and treated accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups: (a) elements (mostly -(i)um); (b) compounds ending in -ide, -in, -ane, -ene, -one, -ol (non-alcoholic), -ose, -an, -ase -> add -um or replace final -e with -um; (c) acids named as acidum + descriptive adjective (acidum sulfuricum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of chemical categories that follow 3rd declension
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemicals ending in -ol (alcohols), -al (aldehydes), -er (ethers/esters), and -yl (organic radicals) are treated as neuter nouns of the 3rd declension with genitive formed by adding -is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of anions ending in -ite and -ate
rubrics_metrics.description: Anions ending in -ite and -ate are treated as masculine nouns of the 3rd declension; English -ite -> Latin -is with genitive -itis; English -ate -> Latin -as with genitive -atis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nitrite -> nitris, nitritis; nitrate -> nitras, nitratis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some chemicals as 1st declension feminine nouns (-a / -ae)
rubrics_metrics.description: A few chemicals (e.g., some drugs and alkaloids) are Latinized in the 1st declension as feminine nouns ending in -a with genitive in -ae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: betaina (-ae), atropina (-ae), adenina (-ae), alanina (-ae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Latinized word stems and genitives for inclusion of chemical names in prokaryote names
rubrics_metrics.description: For use in prokaryote generic names and specific epithets, word stems and genitives of Latinized chemical names are the basis and are then treated like other word elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary names are permitted but must be treated as Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus names or specific epithets may be taken from any source and may even be composed in an arbitrary manner; they must, however, be treated as Latin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cedecea, Afipia, Kordia, Kribbella, Waddlia, Desemzia derived from acronyms like CDC, AFIP, KORDI, KRIBB, WADDL, DSMZ. Specific epithets examples include unamae (from UNAM) and nasdae (from NASDA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for short, elegant, easily spelled/pronounced arbitrary names; indicate gender
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing arbitrary names or epithets, authors should aim at short, elegant, easily spelled and pronounced ones. With arbitrary genus names the gender must also be indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: infrasubspecific subdivision vs infrasubspecific taxon
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish infrasubspecific 'subdivision' (term) from 'taxon'. An infrasubspecific taxon is one strain or a set of strains showing the same or similar properties and treated as a taxonomic group. Infrasubspecific terms refer to kinds of taxa below subspecies (e.g., serovar, chemovar, forma specialis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Infrasubspecific subdivisions are not arranged in any order of rank and may overlap one another. If a species has not been divided into subspecies, infrasubspecific terms may be applied within that species; they remain infrasubspecific for nomenclatural purposes until raised to subspecies or species rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid use of the term 'form' and 'individual' for infrasubspecific designations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infrasubspecific form has been used to refer to a bacterial strain, but this use should be avoided. The term 'individual' has little meaning in bacteriology and is best avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of culture, clone, strain
rubrics_metrics.description: A culture is a population of bacterial cells in a given place at a given time. A clone is a population derived from a single parent cell. A strain is made up of the descendants of a single isolation in pure culture and is usually a succession of cultures, often derived from a single colony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most bacterial strains are not known to be clones. The number of bacteria giving rise to the original colony is often unknown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation to use suffix -var or -form instead of -type for infrasubspecific terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Table 5 contains commonly used infrasubspecific terms; the introduction of the suffix '-var' or '-form' to replace '-type' is recommended to avoid confusion with the strict use of the term 'type' to mean nomenclatural type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'type' in bacteriology should be used strictly for a nomenclatural type (Principle 5 and Chapter 3, Section 4) and not to designate a division of a species or taxa based on antigenic characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'group' is informal only
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'group' is informal and has no nomenclatural standing; it may be useful to designate informally a set of organisms with certain characteristics, but must be used with care and exact definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should not be used to avoid the correct name of a taxon such as genus or species. Example: 'IID group,' later named Cardiobacterium hominis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation format for infrasubspecific taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: An infrasubspecific taxon is designated by the name of the species followed by the infrasubspecific term used to designate this subdivision followed by the infrasubspecific designation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Staphylococcus aureus phagovar 81. Reference strains of infrasubspecific taxa may be designated. Designations may be latinized words, vernacular names, numbers, letters, or formulae (e.g., Xanthomonas translucens f.sp. cerealis; phagovar 42D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature of strains
rubrics_metrics.description: A strain may be designated in any manner, e.g., by the name of an individual, by a locality, or by a number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue of common infrasubspecific terms and their meanings (Table 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide preferred names, synonyms, and notes for common infrasubspecific terms such as biovar (biochemical/physiological properties), chemovar (chemical constitution), cultivar (a cultivated strain with special properties), forma specialis (parasitic/symbiotic microorganism adapted to a host), morphovar (morphological characteristics), pathovar/pathotype (pathogenic reactions), phagovar (reactions to bacteriophage), serovar/serotype (antigenic characteristics), phase (restricted to well-defined stages), state (colonial variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes include preferences (e.g., name a forma specialis preferably by the scientific name of the host in the genitive) and references (see Dye et al. 1980 in Appendix 3 for pathovars).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional status Candidatus: when to use
rubrics_metrics.description: The provisional status 'Candidatus' may be used to record the properties of putative taxa of prokaryotes for which more than a mere nucleic acid sequence is available but for which characteristics required for description according to the Code are lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required in a Candidatus description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of a Candidatus should include: (a) genomic information (nucleic acid sequences apt to determine phylogenetic position); (b) all information so far available on structure and morphology (appropriate illustration), physiology and metabolism, reproductive features, the natural environment in which the organism can be identified by techniques for cell identification; (c) any other available and suitable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 lists items for inclusion such as status, vernacular epithet, phylogenetic lineage, cultivation, Gram reaction, morphology, basis of assignment, specific identification of morphotype, habitat/association/host, metabolism and unusual features, growth temperature, source, authors, essential reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and printing convention for Candidatus names
rubrics_metrics.description: A Candidatus name consists of the word Candidatus followed by a 'vernacular epithet' (a genus name with specific epithet, or only genus name, or only specific epithet). The word Candidatus is printed in italics but the vernacular epithet is not printed in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Candidatus Liberobacter asiaticum; Candidatus magnetobacterium; Candidatus intracellularis. Note: the Candidatus name has no standing in prokaryote nomenclature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidatus registry and subsequent formal naming
rubrics_metrics.description: A codified record (list) of Candidatus organisms is kept by the Judicial Commission of the ICSP in cooperation with the Editorial Board of the IJSEM and published at appropriate intervals. When a Candidatus organism is later isolated and the pure culture sufficiently described, it must be classified and named according to the Rules of the Code and the Candidatus name is deleted from the Candidatus list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: authors planning to describe a Candidatus are recommended to read Murray & Stackebrandt (1995) and Murray & Schleifer (1994).
